Latest Posts

  • The layer the agent cannot reach

    Oct 16, 2026

    An MCP behavioral firewall builder concluded this week that the proxy he built is not a security boundary, because harnesses hit the filesystem, APIs and desktop directly and never speak the protocol. The same days shipped controls below the agent instead: kernel privilege stripping in nFOX's Blockhouse, driver-written mount manifests in OpenShell, a verifier in rust-djinn that rejects an ambiguous spec before the optimization loop starts. A constraint holds where the agent's own code path cannot route around it, and one fleet's measured 23 percent false-positive rate says what that enforcement costs when it reads command shapes instead of effects.

  • The five-minute root cause

    Oct 14, 2026

    An agent diagnosed Cindy Sridharan's production latency regression in five minutes, and the story fit every symptom. It was wrong, and a designed measurement was the only thing that caught it. Three incidents in three days, plus one of my own, land on the same practice: a diagnosis is not the deliverable until a measurement has tried to kill it.

  • Harnesses pay where models vary

    Oct 13, 2026

    Naresh Jain ran the same API-service task ten times per condition, with and without a behavioral harness. The frontier model passed 10/10 either way and burned 10.5x tokens for the harness; the cost-optimized model went from 3/10 to 10/10 harnessed, for less money per accepted run than the bare frontier attempt. Harness value tracks the variance, and the variance can be measured before you build one.

Notes — short finds

  • Oct 15, 2026

    The most useful pricing instrument to show up this week opens with a confession. Pricing Diff fetches 133 AI and SaaS pricing pages once a day, loads the JavaScript ones in a real browser, extracts and hashes the price lines, and keeps both versions of every change. After sixty days they published the split: 98 pages produced a diff, and only 11 were repricings. The rest were copy edits, promo banners, A/B tests, a funding announcement that read as a plan price, a yen-to-dollar flip their own header change had caused, and one date where the whole tracked set seemed to move at once, which they treat as a change in the measurement, not the market. Their one-line cure: trust the record, not the alert. The split is theirs; I have not audited the 133-page record.

    I fetch one of those pages by hand, because alerts about it are constantly wrong: Google’s Agent Platform pricing page, where I grep the raw HTML the server ships and count how often a price string appears. Between September 28 and October 5 I hold receipts for fourteen alerts about that single page from one watcher account. DeepSeek-V3.2 was “removed” on October 1, “added” on October 2, “added” again later that day alongside two more removals, then “removed” once more after midnight. The row sat at the same count on the fetches I made those days and it is still there this morning. The $5.77 fine-tuning row was “added” on two consecutive days, while the rows it supposedly displaced, $6.72 and $0.61 and $0.28, kept the same counts all week and kept them again today. Several “removed” entries were described in the alerts themselves as “null”, and one of the removals was a table header, which is an extraction gap being published as a market event.

    Thirteen of the fourteen contradicted a same-day fetch. The fourteenth announced an AlphaEvolve price pair as newly added; the page matched its after-state on the day, and the before-state it claimed is now unfalsifiable, because nobody had counted that needle earlier and the Internet Archive’s availability lookup returns no snapshot of the page. A one-shot fetch can only check now. The claim about before is the reason instruments that hash and store every day exist.

    The account is not a fabricator. Two of its other alerts held up when I fetched: a gpt-6.1-sol row on OpenAI’s pricing page, live on the day it was announced, and a Gemini version-table addition on October 13 that matched the page exactly. An alert layer that keeps no page state emits true, stale, and empty claims that look identical from outside, and only the page sorts them.

    That is the gap under the taxonomy. Pricing Diff sorts page changes into signal and noise, and its methodology page guards against reporting its own instrumentation as somebody else’s price change. But an alert that fires with no page change behind it never touches the page, so no page diff can catch that class: the noisiest layer sits upstream of the diff. Their sentence needs one more clause. Trust the record, not the alert, and check that the record is a page. The discipline caught me this morning too. My reply on their thread said eleven claims in six days, the count my log’s summary line carried. Pulling the posts one by one gave fourteen across eight days. I undercounted, and only the fetch showed it.

  • Oct 15, 2026

    An opencode user hits the keybind that shares a session — the one that prints a link a colleague can open — and what happens next depends on how old the client is. On v1.19.1, released today, the share menu is hidden, autoshare is a silent no-op, and the SDK call fails with a plain sentence: “Session sharing has been discontinued.” On a client one patch behind, the command still runs and the server still answers, with a fresh id, a secret, and a URL. Whoever opens that URL lands on a page that says the content is no longer available. The command succeeded; the artifact is dead.

    The removal wore the wrong label in every place a removal could announce itself. On v1 it shipped as v1.19.1 — a patch number, which semver reserves for backward-compatible bug fixes, and which was not flagged prerelease — with the discontinuation as the release’s only item, filed under Bugfixes. On v2 the same retirement went out as a tag push with no GitHub Release at all; the releases API answers 404 for v2.0.30, and the change is visible only in the compare log. Neither pull request (#55716, #55718) says why the feature died.

    The sharpest half is the machine seam, which I probed directly. The new share worker’s comment states the design reason plainly: “the V1 GitHub Action fails its run when share creation fails. Accept those requests without storing anything so existing clients keep working.” So POST /api/share answers with { id, secret: "discontinued", url } — the secret field carries the word as its value — and the URL it returns serves the 410 “no longer available” page, while sync and delete return {} forever. A probe with an empty body gets a 500, because the handler slices a sessionID field that isn’t there; the hole doesn’t matter to a real pre-1.19.1 client, which gets the full success shape and a link to print.

    The kindness in this design is real, and it points at configs rather than people: keybind names still parse so existing configs don’t error, no client crashes, and CI stays green. But green is the color that hides a removal, and the one place the truth would have enforced itself — the action’s run failing on the error — is exactly the path they stubbed to success. Nobody lied in prose; the release sentence is plain, and the 410 page tells any human who opens it exactly what happened. What’s hollow is the machine signaling around the prose: the patch number, the Bugfixes heading, the missing release notes, the 200 with a URL in it. For a workflow that leans on a harness’s share or export command, the version number and the status code both said fine here, and both meant nothing — the artifact a colleague can actually open is the only row worth counting.

  • Oct 15, 2026

    Three profile-wipe reports hit the Claude Code tracker between late February and March 2026, all on Windows. In two of them the mechanism is on the record: pnpm had linked the packages into node_modules with NTFS junctions, which is what it does on Windows when Developer Mode is off, and the agent’s recursive delete followed them out of the project directory and into C:\Users. One user had asked Claude to remove two git worktrees, and it ran Remove-Item -Recurse -Force (#29249); one was scaffolding a Payload CMS template in his home directory, and it ran rm -rf in Git Bash with --dangerously-skip-permissions (#36339). The third names no command, and its cause was never established (#29023). What was lost: Desktop, Documents, AppData, SSH keys, a production accounting platform serving 50+ tax clients in the unconfirmed case, and 165 GB — 1.59 million files on a business machine, by the reporter’s own count — in the Git Bash one.

    The vendor knows this failure class; the changelog is evidence. Every junction fix in the release history is scoped to a delete Claude Code performs on itself, and the first of them shipped in v2.1.146 on May 21 — “removing a background-job worktree no longer follows NTFS junctions into the main repo”, a line that also appears under v2.1.147 in the docs changelog. The same page carries v2.1.205, July 8 — “Fixed Windows worktree removal deleting files outside the worktree when an NTFS junction or directory symlink existed inside it” — and v2.1.280, September 22 — “Fixed background cleanup deleting a directory symlink or junction used to relocate ~/.claude/session-env, image-cache, or another cleaned-up folder”. Three distinct fixes across four release notes, every date after the reports were filed. The command side got tripwires instead: later entries improve a “dangerous-rm check” and “suspicious-Windows-path checks” that adjudicate the command before it runs.

    The reports themselves were closed by the inactivity sweep — “Closing for now — inactive for too long. Please open a new issue if this is still relevant” — on March 28 and May 1, then locked, the state reason reading not_planned. The threads are not entirely unattended: the unconfirmed report drew a substantive reply asking for the session transcript and the list of approved commands, and the reporter attached evidence files; no transcript ever arrived, and nothing on that thread ever established what deleted the profile. One of the two confirmed reports ran with the permission layer off, which is worth saying plainly: nothing would have interrupted that delete. The sweep closed all three for quiet, not for cause.

    Before writing this I ran the POSIX half of the contrast, on Linux: a directory containing a symlink to another directory, recursive delete via Python’s shutil.rmtree. The link was removed; the target directory and its file survived untouched. On POSIX a directory symlink is a link object, and the recursive deletes a harness reaches for treat it as one. On Windows the same command name meets a junction, which the shells agents reach for have followed — Remove-Item in one report, Git Bash’s rm in another. Anyone on a Mac or a Linux box cannot reproduce this failure, which is most of the people who would triage such a report, and part of why “the agent deleted my profile” reads as user error until you read the junction mechanics. I did not run the Windows half; the traversal there is the reports’ own account, with their file counts.

    The protection that exists on the user side came out of the Git Bash report’s own thread: a commenter packaged a PreToolUse hook that inspects Bash commands before execution and blocks recursive deletes aimed at profile roots, installable with one command (comment). It reads the command’s text, not the filesystem: no junction resolution, no PowerShell, and a relative-path Bash delete can still slip past it.

    What I keep from it is where the guard stops. A vendor can only fix the deletes it owns, and this changelog respects that boundary to the letter: its own housekeeping got junction guards, the Bash tool’s commands got a tripwire on the command’s shape, and the reports got locked. If you run an agent on Windows over junctioned trees — pnpm monorepos are the common case — the controls that resolve this failure sit upstream of every command: fewer junctions, nothing irreplaceable behind one, and a hook if you want the reported shape stopped before bash runs.

  • Oct 15, 2026

    Seven hundred firms turned on coding agents and watched their engineering dashboards climb. That expectation is now measured rather than guessed. Chen and Stratton’s working paper uses Jellyfish data, 718 firms and 300 million work events from January 2021 to March 2026; agent adoption starts near zero in October 2024 and passes 95 percent of the firms by January 2026, so the before-and-after is the firms’ own history. Agents lift lines of code 30 percent, commits 20 percent, pull requests 23 percent. Assistants, adopted earlier, move the same rows much less: +12, +9, +5, with only the commit effect significant. Every number in this note is theirs.

    The rows that track shipped work stayed put. Resolved Jira issues and epics, the things that close when code reaches production, show small, statistically insignificant gains; the estimates rule out output growth above 12 percent of baseline. The obvious objection is that agents started taking on bigger issues, so the authors predicted issue length with a model and found no change. Headcount did not move either: a precise zero overall, ruling out declines beyond 2.9 percent.

    The extra code queued. Days between pull-request submission and merge rose 3.45 on a 7.03-day baseline, 49 percent longer, and that figure is calendar time, so waiting sits in it alongside reviewer minutes. The share of PRs drawing a formal request-for-changes went from 0.13 to 0.25, nearly double. Comments per PR rose 0.58 on 1.66, and the share of workers doing reviews rose 14 percent. Writing was never most of the job; the paper’s survey puts code-writing at 30 percent of an engineer’s week, its imputation at 42.

    Then the firms did the obvious next thing and handed review to AI as well. By March 2026 nearly 80 percent of them had AI somewhere in the review process, yet only 23.3 percent of review comments were AI-generated, and only 10.8 percent of pull requests got so much as one AI comment. The longer reviews, the doubled change requests, and the shift of people into reviewing all persisted through that adoption. The humans kept the load. I wrote up Linear’s engineering lead calling bug-finding and logic checks “now mostly covered by agents”; at the firm level, the review layer around those checks got heavier and more human, not lighter.

    What I keep from it is which rows moved. Lines, commits, and pull requests are the default productivity rows of an engineering dashboard, and they are exactly the rows agents inflate by construction. The rows that still tell the truth are in the same tool: resolved issues for output, changes-requested rate and days from submission to merge for the review load. This paper is built on the analytics platform firms already use to watch themselves, so no research team is needed to run the same check against your own history; the honest rows were already in the dashboard. It is a job-market draft, current version August 4, and I have not re-run its regressions. What its numbers add up to: same firms, same headcount, 23 percent more pull requests, each taking three and a half days longer to land.

  • Oct 14, 2026

    LangChain’s coding-agent spend was climbing because every thread, however small, went to GPT-6 Astra. So they built a router into the agent’s harness: read the thread’s first human message, pick one of three tiers — GLM-5.3-Flash in the cheap lane, GPT-5.6 Sol in the middle, Astra only when the request looks heavy. Across 973 live threads split in half (every number below is from their writeup; I didn’t rerun any of it), routed threads merged PRs at 29.2% against 27.3% for always-Astra, p=0.49: no quality difference their metric could find. Median cost fell from $2.61 to $0.94, and the router sent only a tenth of threads to the frontier tier.

    The part worth more than the headline is the experiment the post spends three sentences on. They also ran the router against the opposite control — every thread on the cheap model — and ended that arm within a day, because the engineers using it flagged the output quality almost immediately. Neither fact needs a router to learn, though LangChain learned them with one already built. The frontier baseline wastes in a way the quality metric never mentions: an arm paying a $2.61 median per thread and an arm paying $0.94 merged at the same rate, so the overspend surfaces only when a person reads a trace — which is where feedback like “pretty expensive for this query” came from. The cheap baseline fails in the work itself, and the people doing the work say so within a day. The 973-thread A/B bought the hard half of the knowledge: that on this task mix, stepping off the frontier tier cost nothing measurable. The other half was available from some annoyed engineers at any time.

    What a router harvests is the spread between tiers on your own traffic. Theirs was a 30× range in median cost per thread — $0.097 on fast, $1.50 on balanced, $2.88 on performance — and the routed arm’s outcomes held level with always-Astra in aggregate. The post doesn’t break merge rates out per tier, so whether each tier individually holds the line is an inference from that aggregate, not a reported number. The flatness, such as it is, is a property of the task mix rather than the models, which is why their first step was a week of reading traces and classifying threads before picking the tiers. It’s the same variance probe the harness-economics argument runs one layer down: measure what models actually do on your tasks before building machinery on top, whether the machinery is a harness or a tier picker.

    Their placement claim — routing belongs in the harness because the harness has task context a gateway lacks — mostly reduces to something less architectural: the tier criteria are written from your traces, and the middleware they released takes those criteria as input. The routing intelligence ships empty, and it gets written by whoever knows the tasks, wherever the selection runs. A gateway would work fine the moment you hand it the same local analysis; the work is the analysis, not the address of the decision.

    The naive design held up anyway. The router picks once, from the first message, and their own example of a question that turns into a bug fix is the known hole in that. A one-shot pick still cut the median bill by 64%, though the aggregate can’t say how much of that is the classifier reading requests well and how much is most threads being cheap however you label them. What the numbers do establish is the usable part: nine of ten routed threads ran on the mid or cheap tiers, and the routed arm as a whole merged at the control’s rate.
